question: The trade agreement being negotiated between the European Union and the Mercosur countries raises many questions and concerns, especially among European food producers. In view of the clear risk that this agreement could cause a wave of inequalities in agriculture, I would like to request a response on a number of key issues: 1.
What safeguard mechanisms does the Commission envisage to protect the interests of European farmers?

Given the requirements of the Green Deal and the numerous restrictions imposed on European food producers, questions are being raised about the balance of the rules. Does the draft agreement impose the same restrictive standards – concerning environmental protection, greenhouse gas emissions, the use of fertilisers and forest protection – on Mercosur food producers?

If the agreement with Mercosur provides for different safety standards and permissible technologies for food production or fertilisers to the standards applied in the EU, why are double standards being applied, putting EU consumers’ health at risk?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.3.2025) The EU is the world’s largest exporter of agri-food products, with a trade surplus of EUR 70 billion in 2023. This is also thanks to its network of trade agreements.

Mercosur is a large and highly protected market with great potential for high quality European agri-food exports such as some dairy products, processed foods, olive oil, malt, some fruits, wines, spirits and nonalcoholic beverages.

Regarding sensitive EU agricultural products, such as beef and poultry, the EU has negotiated limited concessions in the form of tariff rate quotas that represent a small fraction of EU consumption. These partial openings will be introduced in gradual stages to allow for a smooth transition. They will be coupled with safeguard clauses to protect the EU market in case imports from Mercosur would cause serious injury.

As regards standards, the EU has negotiated legally binding chapters on trade and sustainable development in all recent comprehensive trade agreements to ensure EU trading partners implement strong labour and environmental commitments. In addition, the EU Deforestation Regulation1 requires that certain commodities to be placed on the EU market must originate from non-deforested areas.

Finally, as regards health and safety the EU’s sanitary and phytosanitary standards are nonnegotiable and are not affected by this or any other trade agreement. The decisions that the EU takes to protect its production and its consumers are underpinned by risk assessments, which are performed by the European Food Safety Authority.
Imported products must always comply with the EU’s stringent food safety requirements regardless of the existence of a trade agreement with the exporting country.
1 Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on the making

available on the Union market and the export from the Union of certain commodities and products associated with deforestation and forest degradation; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1115
